edges.description: Loss of FIG4 lowers cellular PI(3,5)P2, because FIG4 is needed to hold the PI(3,5)P2-synthesizing complex together.
The genotype-phenotype comparison with CMT4J shows that complete absence of FIG4 activity, not partial loss, is what produces central nervous system disease.

edges.description: Complete absence of FIG4 activity produces extensive skeletal anomalies; the intermediates between PI(3,5)P2 loss and the digital and clavicular aplasia are not known.
FIG4 binds PIKFYVE through VAC14, and every subunit of the complex is required for PI(3,5)P2 synthesis.
With PI(3,5)P2 deficient, TRPML1-mediated lysosomal calcium efflux is suppressed, intralysosomal calcium rises, dynamin-1 is downregulated, and lysosomes fail to undergo fission.
PI(3,5)P2-deficient neurons and astrocytes accumulate LC3-II, p62 and LAMP-2, indicating a block in autolysosome formation or recycling.
Restoring lysosomal calcium efflux rescues the abnormal lysosomal storage, placing the fission defect upstream of the vacuoles.
Inclusion bodies accumulate in the brain regions that go on to degenerate.
Neurons of Fig4-null mice contain enlarged endolysosomal vacuoles in the same brain regions that degenerate; neuronal Fig4 expression prevents both.
The skeletal muscle vacuoles are of the lysosomal storage type seen in other tissues.

Both case reports that found abnormal urinary oligosaccharides also found lysosomal-type storage vacuoles and interpreted the excretion as part of a lysosomal storage process; the oligosaccharide has not been identified and the link is inferred rather than demonstrated.
Fig4-null osteoblasts accumulate large vacuoles, and reduced bone formation with normal osteoclasts is interpreted by the authors as osteoblast dysfunction secondary to lysosomal dysfunction.
